client: I've been really struggling since my grandmother passed away last month. Every time there's a family get-together, I just can't seem to enjoy it — it feels like there's this huge empty space where she used to be, and I can't stop thinking about her. I'm not even sure talking about it is going to change anything, but I figured I'd give this a try.
therapist: It takes real courage to reach out, especially when part of you isn't sure it will help — and I'm really glad you did. The emptiness you're describing at those family gatherings makes so much sense; your grandmother was clearly a meaningful presence, and her absence leaves a very real gap that others around you might not fully see. I'd love to understand a little more about what those moments feel like for you — when you're at a gathering and that wave of missing her comes, what kinds of thoughts tend to run through your mind?

client: It's like... I'll be sitting there at the table, surrounded by everyone talking and laughing, and I just keep thinking "she should be here, she would have loved this." And then almost immediately I feel this guilt, like maybe I'm ruining the moment for myself or being ungrateful that everyone else is there. It's hard to explain because on the outside I'm probably smiling and nodding, but inside I feel completely alone in a room full of people who are supposed to be my family.
therapist: That image of smiling on the outside while feeling completely alone on the inside is such a poignant one, and it makes sense that carrying both of those things at once would be exhausting. I want to gently notice something — you're grieving your grandmother, which is a completely natural and loving response, and yet your mind is turning that grief into evidence that *you're* somehow doing something wrong by feeling it. What do you think your grandmother would say if she could see you in that moment, missing her at the table?

client: That question kind of caught me off guard, honestly. I think she would have wanted me to let myself feel it, she was never someone who told you to push things down. But then there's this other voice that says I'm being self-indulgent, like everyone else at that table had lost her too and they were managing to hold it together, so why couldn't I.
therapist: It's really meaningful that you could hear your grandmother's voice so clearly there — she sounds like someone who gave you permission to be human. That critical voice comparing you to others at the table is worth examining though, because it's making a big assumption: that "holding it together" on the outside means people aren't struggling on the inside — which is exactly what *you* were doing just moments ago. What if some of the people at that table were quietly carrying the same weight you were, just behind their own smiles?

client: That's... actually a weird thought to sit with, because part of me wants to believe it, but another part of me is like, no, they genuinely have their lives more figured out than I do. Like, it's not just a feeling — some of them actually do have stable jobs and relationships and all the things I don't have yet. But I guess I'm also realizing that I was sitting there looking completely fine on the outside while feeling like I was falling apart inside, so maybe you have a point that I can't really know what's going on for them either.
therapist: There's something really important happening right now — you just caught your own mind in the act, and that's no small thing. You noticed that you were using visible markers like jobs and relationships to assume others have it "more figured out," while knowing firsthand that your own visible calm was hiding something completely different. I'm curious — when you compare yourself to them and feel like you're falling behind, do you think that's a new feeling that grief has brought up, or does it feel like something that was already there before you lost your grandmother?

client: Honestly, I think it was already there before she died — I've always been someone who looks around and feels like everyone else got a manual I never received. But losing her kind of turned up the volume on it, like grief stripped away whatever was muffling that feeling before. She was actually one of the few people who made me feel like I wasn't behind, and now that she's gone, that voice comparing me to everyone else just gets so much louder.
therapist: What you just described is such an important insight — your grandmother wasn't just someone you loved, she was also a voice that genuinely countered that deep feeling of being behind, and losing her means losing that anchor too. It makes so much sense that the grief and that older wound are now tangled together, because in a way you lost her twice — once as a person, and once as the one who helped quiet that critical voice. I'm wondering, when she made you feel like you weren't behind — what was it she actually said or did that allowed you to believe it, even temporarily?

client: It's a good question, and I've been sitting with it for a second because I want to get it right. She never really said anything grand or philosophical — it was more like she'd ask me what I'd been up to, and when I told her, she'd just... light up. Like genuinely, not in a polite way, and she'd say something like "see, you're doing just fine" in this matter-of-fact tone that made it feel true instead of like empty reassurance. I think what made it land was that she actually knew me, so it didn't feel like she was just saying it to make me feel better.
therapist: There's something so tender and specific about what you just described — it wasn't grand words, it was her genuine delight in *you*, and the fact that it came from someone who truly knew you is exactly what made it feel like truth rather than comfort. In a way, you've just identified something really important: you're not someone who can't be reached by that reassurance, you're someone who needs it to come from a place of real knowing — and that's not a flaw, that's actually quite wise. I'm curious, are there any other people in your life right now who know you well enough that their belief in you might carry some of that same weight, even if it feels different from hers?

client: I sat with that for a moment because it actually did feel true, what you said about needing it to come from real knowing. But when I try to think of who else might carry that kind of weight right now, I honestly draw a blank, and that feels kind of devastating to admit out loud. My sister maybe, but we've grown apart since mom died and I'm not sure she really sees me the way she used to.
therapist: Saying that out loud clearly took something, and I want you to know that the ache in admitting it makes complete sense — recognizing a gap where connection used to be is its own kind of grief. What strikes me is that your sister didn't disappear from your answer entirely; she came to mind first, even with the distance between you, which suggests there might still be something alive there worth paying attention to. I'm wondering — when you say she doesn't see you the way she used to, do you think that's something that drifted gradually, or is there a moment where you felt the two of you stopped really knowing each other?

client: I think it drifted, mostly, but there was this one Thanksgiving maybe three years ago where I said something about feeling overwhelmed with work and she kind of brushed it off, made a joke about it, and I remember thinking "she doesn't really want to hear this." After that I just... stopped offering those parts of myself to her. I guess I built a wall without really deciding to, and now I don't know how to take it down even if I wanted to.
therapist: That one moment at Thanksgiving carried so much weight — it became a rule your mind wrote about what your sister could and couldn't hold, and then quietly, without a grand decision, you started protecting yourself by pulling back. It's worth noticing that she may not even know that moment landed the way it did, which means the distance between you might be built on a misread rather than a true reflection of what she's capable of now. I'm curious — if you imagine a version of things where that wall could come down a little, what feels like the scariest part of letting her see you again?

client: The scariest part is probably that she'd see how much I'm actually struggling and then just... not know what to do with it, or worse, say something that makes it worse without meaning to. That's kind of what happened at Thanksgiving — I don't think she meant to make me feel small, but she did, and I spent weeks replaying it. So even if you're right that she might not realize how that landed, it doesn't really make me feel safer about trying again.
therapist: That fear makes complete sense — you're not being irrational, you're protecting yourself based on real experience, and the fact that you spent weeks replaying that moment shows just how much it mattered to you. What I notice though is that the risk you're describing isn't really "will she hurt me," it's more "can she handle the real me" — and that's a question you haven't actually been able to test since you stopped offering those parts of yourself to her. I'm wondering, is there a version of reaching out that feels small enough to be survivable — not the whole wall coming down at once, but maybe just a crack of light?

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me actually wants to believe that framing... but I keep thinking, what if I offer just a small piece and she still doesn't get it, or worse, she makes it weird? That almost feels more painful than staying closed off, because then I'd have actual proof instead of just fear. I guess a small thing feels safer in theory, but I can't figure out what that would even look like with her.
therapist: What you're naming is actually a really honest tension — right now the uncertainty is painful, but it also protects you from something feeling final, and part of you isn't sure trading fear for proof is a good deal. That makes a lot of sense, and it's worth sitting with rather than rushing past. I'm wondering — if you think about the last time you and your sister were just *together* without anything heavy on the table, what did that look like, and is there any version of that kind of ordinary moment that might be a doorway back in?
